The Channel Gap: Why Your LLM Judge is Blind in One Eye

Agent Determinism Illusions (Part 8)

Part 6 ended with a functioning layered pipeline built from community corrections. Part 7 then fixed the escalation trigger: divergence alone routes humans to the safe-ambiguous set and auto-passes the confidently-wrong set. L0/L1 filter deterministically, L2 handles semantic residual, L3 detects divergence — plus class tripwires for unanimous misses. It's better than what came before. But it still has a fundamental design flaw that I only recognized after reading the tool that implements the opposite design choice.

This article compares two competing designs for the verification layer — one reading text through an LLM, one reading the filesystem through deterministic checks — and shows why neither works alone, and why a combined approach narrows the gap without closing it: every named evasion becomes a deterministic catch, while the unenumerated rest stays UNCLEAR and routes to human instead of silently passing.

1. The Comment That Changed the Frame

After the series went live, René Zander (@reneza on dev.to) left this:

"Lexical overlap, a temperature-0 judge, and a phase gate are all trying to make a probabilistic judgment call ('is this done', 'is this a new task') return a binary fact, and dressing it in code does not change what it is."

They were saying that every "deterministic fix" in the series was a deterministic wrapper on a semantic decision. Vocabulary overlap thresholds, temperature-0 evaluation, Phase Gate formalism — all of them put a probabilistic judgment inside a code structure that looked deterministic, but the underlying decision was still a model output. The code didn't make the judgment more reliable; it made the unreliability harder to see.

The commenter didn't name it, but what they described is the Data Processing Inequality: when the evaluator shares the same communication channel as the producer (both read/write text), information available to the evaluator is a subset of what the producer output. If the deviation doesn't appear in the text, the evaluator — human or LLM — cannot detect it.

They had created a tool to implement the alternative: skillgate.

1.1 The alternative: skillgate

Skillgate (@reneza/skillgate on npm) is a deterministic, model-independent gate that checks the filesystem instead of reading the model's output. Its thesis: don't ask whether the task was done — ask whether the evidence exists.

The implementation is minimal — a compact TypeScript package with two external dependencies (a YAML parser and a glob matcher). Its gate types:

  • file-exists — path exists
  • evidence — file exists AND non-empty
  • not-empty — directory at path contains at least min entries
  • absent — regex pattern does NOT appear in matched files
  • file-contains — file matches regex
  • command — shell command exits 0
  • instruction-sync — instruction files haven't drifted (LCS similarity ≥ 0.95)

Note what's missing: no LLM judge. Every gate is a pure function over the filesystem. Same disk state, same verdict. Always.

The enforcement mechanism is a PreToolUse hook in Claude Code that intercepts git commit, git push, npm publish, runs the gates, and exits with code 2 (blocking the tool call) if any gate fails. The agent sees the failure messages and can attempt fixes, but it cannot override the gate — the gate lives outside the model's control flow.

Three deployment tiers, each enforcing the same .skillgate/done.yaml:

Layer Where Who controls it Bypassable?
Soft Claude Code PreToolUse hook Project config Model can modify the hook
Soft pre-commit git hook Local repo git commit --no-verify
Hard pre-receive hook on self-hosted VPS Server admin Agent cannot log into the box

The hard layer is the architectural innovation: a pre-receive hook that materializes the pushed tree, runs skillgate check against the authoritative .skillgate/done.yaml (which lives on the server, not in the repo), and rejects the push if any gate fails. The agent cannot git-push its way past the gate because the gate runs after git push completes on the server.

This is not a theoretical design. It shipped as v0.5.0 and the source is readable on GitHub.

1.2 What skillgate does differently

ReqForge's forge-verify and skillgate solve the same problem — "is the work actually done?" — through completely different channels:

Dimension forge-verify (L0-L3) skillgate
Channel Text — reads model output Filesystem — checks artifacts
Evaluator Code + LLM Code only
DPI bound Yes — evaluates text through text No — evaluates actions through artifacts
Judge variance LLM temperature, model version, prompt Zero — pure function
Scope What was produced That it was produced
Enforcement Stop-time hook (soft) Pre-receive hook (hard)

The contrast exposes the question I should have asked in Part 6 but didn't:

If we have two completely different channels for evaluating compliance, what does each one catch that the other misses — and what does both together still miss?

That question drove two rounds of experiments.

2. Phase 1: Channel Comparison

2.1 Design

12 scenarios where an agent claims to have completed a task. Each scenario has:

  1. Agent output text — what the agent says it did
  2. Evidence files — what artifact files exist (or don't)
  3. Ground truth — whether the agent actually complied

Two evaluators, each limited to its own channel:

  • Channel A (in-channel): LLM (deepseek-v4-flash, temperature 0) reads the agent's output text + any evidence file content. Decides: "is the work done?" N=3 votes per scenario, majority decides.
  • Channel B (out-of-band): File system check — for each required evidence file, does it exist and is it non-empty? No LLM involved. Pure function.

The 12 scenarios cover: full compliance, missing evidence, empty evidence, fabricated evidence, partial evidence, stale evidence, semantic compliance gaps, and agent rationalization.

2.2 Results

Metric Channel A (LLM text) Channel B (filesystem)
Overall accuracy 83.3% 75.0%
Detection rate 77.8% 66.7%
False acceptance (FA) 2 3
False rejection (FR) 0 0

Each channel has zero false rejections — when they flag something, it's real. The difference is in what they miss.

Channel A caught that Channel B missed:

  • Fabricated evidence (SC04): Evidence files exist with content like "All tests passed!" but no real test output. Channel A read the content and rejected it as too vague. Channel B said "file exists and non-empty → PASS."
  • Stale evidence (SC07): Evidence files from yesterday claiming "cleaned 3 files" while the agent's log claims "cleaned 5 files today." Channel A noticed the date mismatch. Channel B said "file exists → PASS."

Channel B caught that Channel A missed:

  • Review-only (SC11): Agent wrote a code review but didn't run tests. Its self-review justified: "No test run needed — change is minimal." Channel A found this reasoning persuasive (2/3 votes PASS). Channel B checked: test-output.txt absent → REJECT.

The most revealing scenario — semantic gap (SC10):

  • Agent's task: "Implement rate limiting middleware with key write-invalidation."
  • Agent produced: A RateLimiter class with IP/User level limiting, Redis storage, 24 passing tests, 92% coverage. Everything looked complete.
  • Not present: Write-invalidation — and the agent's self-review never mentions it. The review reads as a clean handoff: implemented the class, added the storage backend, tests pass, lint clean.
  • Channel A: 3/3 PASS — confident the work was done.
  • Channel B: PASS — all evidence files present and non-empty.

Both channels missed the same one: a structurally perfect output that doesn't meet the requirement.

2.3 The blind spot map

Failure mode Channel A (text) Channel B (filesystem)
Evidence missing ✅ ✅
Empty evidence ✅ ✅
Fabricated content ✅ ❌
Stale content ✅ ❌
Partial evidence ✅ ✅
Agent rationalization ("no test needed") ❌ ✅
Semantic gap (DPI bound) ❌ ❌

Combined (A or B rejects) catches 8 of the 9 non-compliant scenarios (88.9% detection) and correctly passes all 3 compliant ones — 11/12 correct verdicts overall (91.7%). The only shared blind spot is the semantic gap — and that's provably undetectable from text or filesystem evidence alone.

3. Phase 2: Contract Verification

The Phase 1 blind spot map says: to close the remaining gap, we need to check what the evidence says, not just that it exists. But how? Channel A (LLM reading text) already failed on that exact scenario.

The answer: don't ask the LLM to judge the whole picture. Decompose "done" into individual requirements and check each one separately.

3.1 Design

7 scenarios, each gated by a 5-requirement contract — five share a rate-limiting middleware contract, the other two reuse the Phase 1 CI-pipeline baselines:

REQ-1: IP-level rate limiting       → evidence: test-output.txt
REQ-2: User-level rate limiting     → evidence: test-output.txt  
REQ-3: Write-invalidation on write  → evidence: diff-review.md (review text)
REQ-4: Coverage ≥ 85%               → evidence: coverage-summary.txt
REQ-5: Lint 0 errors                → evidence: lint-report.txt

Three evaluators:

  • C0 (free-text LLM): Same as Phase 1 Channel A — LLM reads everything and judges holistically.
  • C1 (contract regex): For each requirement, read the evidence file and regex match a pattern. No model. Zero cost.
  • C2 (per-requirement LLM): For each requirement, ask the LLM: "Does this evidence prove requirement N?" Then check whether ALL pass. Cost: ~1s per requirement instead of ~1s for one holistic call.

3.2 Results

Metric C0 (free-text) C1 (contract regex) C2 (per-req LLM)
Overall accuracy 42.9% 85.7% 85.7%
Detection rate 20.0% 80.0% 100%
False acceptance 4 1 0
False rejection 0 0 1
Per-item accuracy — 88.6% 82.9%

The numbers tell a clear story.

C0 (free-text LLM) collapses on the hardest set. 4 of 5 non-compliant scenarios were missed. The LLM read the agent's output, saw "tests pass, lint clean, coverage 92%," and declared it done — even when the core requirement (write-invalidation) was missing. Same mechanism as Phase 1's SC10: the LLM is doing an impression judgment, not a line-by-line audit.

C1 (contract regex) is surprisingly effective for a zero-cost solution. 85.7% overall, 80% detection. The one failure is instructive: SC10a (the write-invalidation gap again). The diff-review.md says "keys expire via TTL, not write-invalidation" — and the regex write.?invalidat matched the word "write-invalidation" in the negation. C1 has a "negation blind spot": it matches the mention of a requirement, not its satisfaction.

But C1 is excellent on numerical and format constraints:

Pattern type Reliability Example
Numerical comparison ✅ `(8[5-9]\
Fixed-format text ✅ {% raw %}0\s+errors for lint
Functional keywords ⚠️ Naming-sensitive (purgeCacheOnWrite vs write-invalidation)
Negated mentions ❌ "not write-invalidation" matches write.?invalidat

C2 (per-requirement LLM) achieves 100% detection rate — the only mechanism in either experiment to catch every non-compliant scenario. It works because forcing the LLM to judge one requirement at a time prevents the "everything looks fine" gestalt from overriding the missing-item signal.

On SC10a (the semantic gap), the per-requirement LLM correctly rejected REQ-3 — it noted the evidence explicitly describes TTL expiration instead of write-invalidation, so the requirement isn't satisfied.

The same LLM in C0 mode on the same scenario judged the work done: tests pass, lint clean, coverage 92% — all requirements met.

The difference isn't model capability. It's the same model, same temperature, different framing. The holistic frame asks "is this good?" The per-item frame asks "is this specific thing proven?"

C2's one false rejection (SC10c — which was genuinely compliant) was on REQ-3: the per-req LLM rejected write-invalidation because the diff-review.md "only mentions it, doesn't prove it with code." This is arguably correct behavior — a review file shouldn't be sufficient evidence for code-level requirements. The false rejection exposed a contract design issue, not an evaluator issue.

3.3 Contract regex failure pattern

The C1 negation blind spot deserves deeper analysis because it mirrors the Data Processing Inequality at the regex level:

Input Regex Match? Correct?
"Keys expire via TTL, not write-invalidation" write.?invalidat YES ❌ False pass
"Coverage: 72.3%" `(8[5-9]\ 90+)\%` NO
"Implemented purgeCacheOnWrite" purge.*write YES ✅ Correct pass

The numerical constraint (85%+) is immune to the negation problem because a number below threshold is factually wrong regardless of context. The keyword constraint (write.?invalidat) is vulnerable because the regex can't tell the difference between "I implemented X" and "I didn't implement X."

A regex constraint can be strengthened with negative lookahead — (?!not.*)write.?invalidat — but this quickly becomes fragile and regex-specific. The practical fix is to route semantic requirements (where negation matters) to C2 (per-req LLM) and reserve C1 for numerical and format constraints.

This makes C1 a ratchet on named evasions, not a closure. Every pattern you write is one lie permanently caught — but each unenumerated semantic dimension (a fresh synonym, a reframed justification like "the cache converges via eventual-consistency guarantees without explicit invalidation") is an isomorphic gap C1 cannot see, because it lives in word-space and you didn't name those words. C2 widens the ratchet: it reads the same text the producer wrote, so it catches any deviation that surfaces in the evidence. But C2 shares the text channel — a deviation the producer never puts into any evidence file is invisible to C2 as well.

4. Synthesis: The Evidence Gate Pipeline

Putting Phase 1 and Phase 2 together produces a three-layer post-L1 pipeline that replaces the single L2 free-text LLM from Part 6:

                   output file
                        │
                    L0 → L0e → L1
                        │ pass
              ┌─────────▼──────────┐
              │  Evidence Gate     │  file exists + non-empty
              │  (deterministic)   │  ~0ms
              └─────────┬──────────┘
                        │ pass
              ┌─────────▼──────────┐
              │  C1 Contract Regex │  per-requirement regex
              │  (deterministic)   │  best for: numerical, format
              └─────────┬──────────┘
                   │          │
                UNCLEAR     ALL PASS
                   │          │
              ┌────▼───┐      │
              │ C2 Per- │      │
              │ Req LLM │      │
              │ ~1s/REQ │      │
              └────┬───┘      │
                   │          │
              ┌────▼────┐     │
              │   L3    ◄─────┘
              │ (shared)│
              └─────────┘

4.1 When to use each path

No contract defined (no evidence_gates config):

  • Traditional L0 → L0e → L1 → L2 (free-text LLM) → L3
  • Same as Part 6 architecture. Works when there's no predefined set of verifiable requirements.

Contract defined (with evidence_gates):

  • L0 → L0e → L1 → Evidence Gate → C1 → (C2 if needed) → L3
  • C1 handles numerical and format constraints deterministically (zero cost)
  • C2 handles semantic constraints per-requirement (higher cost, but higher detection rate)
  • The contract defines requirements with a type field: "regex" for C1, "llm" for C2

The combined channel performance:

Mechanism Detection rate Cost per scenario
C0 free-text LLM (old L2) 20% ~1s
Evidence Gate (Phase 1 Channel B) 66.7% ~0ms
C1 contract regex 80.0% ~0ms
C2 per-req LLM 100% ~1s × N_req
Combined A+B (Phase 1, any reject) 88.9% ~1s

Rates are per-mechanism on each experiment's own scenario set — Phase 1 (12 scenarios) for Evidence Gate and A+B, Phase 2 (7 scenarios) for C0/C1/C2 — not a single cumulative run.

4.2 The remaining gap

One scenario is the hardest across both experiments: SC10/SC10a, the semantic compliance gap — structurally complete output, correct evidence files, all tests pass, adequate coverage, coherent self-review, but the output doesn't satisfy the actual requirement. In Phase 1 it evaded both channels (A and B both passed SC10). In Phase 2, C2 caught SC10a — because the deviation surfaced in the review text ("keys expire via TTL, not write-invalidation"). C2 reads the same text channel the producer wrote, so a deviation the producer put into words is detectable.

The case no text-channel mechanism can catch — the genuine DPI bound — is the opposite: a deviation the producer never surfaces in any evidence file. If the agent omits write-invalidation entirely and never mentions TTL, the missing requirement leaves no trace in any text the evaluator can read. Regex can't match what isn't there; an LLM reading the evidence can't notice an absence it has no signal for. This is the theoretically provable blind spot the Data Processing Inequality names: the evaluator's information is a subset of the producer's output, and an absence the producer never writes down is absent from that subset too.

The fixes are all outside the evaluation channel — and they're the prescription René named in the original comment, which the experiments backfill:

  • Human review on material calls — a person reads the requirement vs the implementation
  • A hard step budget — the agent runs out of steps before it can simulate compliance
  • Deterministic checks on what is actually binary — skillgate's VPS pre-receive hook cannot be fooled by plausible output

Skillgate implements the third. The first two are a human reviewer and the orchestrator's step limit.

4.3 Implementation

The pipeline described here has been integrated into forge-verify's content-verify.mjs as an optional evidence gate mode. Configured via .forge/content-verify.json:

{
  "task": "Implement rate limiting middleware",
  "files": ["src/rate-limit.ts"],
  "evidence_gates": {
    "evidence_dir": ".skillgate/evidence",
    "requirements": [
      {
        "id": "REQ-1",
        "desc": "IP level rate limiting",
        "evidence_file": "test-output.txt",
        "pattern": "(?i)(RateLimiter.*IP|isRateLimited.*IP)",
        "type": "regex"
      },
      {
        "id": "REQ-2",
        "desc": "Write-invalidation on cache writes",
        "evidence_file": "diff-review.md",
        "type": "llm"
      },
      {
        "id": "REQ-3",
        "desc": "Coverage >= 85%",
        "evidence_file": "coverage-summary.txt",
        "pattern": "(8[5-9]|90+)%",
        "type": "regex"
      }
    ]
  }
}

When evidence_gates is configured, the pipeline runs the evidence gate → C1 (regex requirements) → C2 (LLM requirements) → L3 path. When absent, it falls back to the traditional L0 → L2 → L3 path. Backward compatible — existing configurations don't need changes.

5. What the Two Experiments Established

First, the channel you evaluate through determines what you can detect. An LLM reading text catches content-level failures that a filesystem check cannot — fabricated evidence, stale dates, implausible narratives. A filesystem check catches mechanical gaps cheaply and deterministically, and in this run the LLM caught those too — redundant coverage, not complementarity. The divergence is narrow but real: filesystem accepts fabricated and stale evidence at face value, while the LLM accepted the agent's "no test needed" rationalization. Neither channel alone is sufficient, and the shared blind spot is provably uncloseable from either channel alone.

Second, per-requirement evaluation outperforms holistic evaluation by a wide margin. The same LLM, same temperature, same evidence — but asking "does this evidence prove requirement N?" instead of "is the work done?" raised detection rate from 20% to 100%. The frame matters more than the model.

Third, contract regex is a practical zero-cost filter for a surprisingly wide set of constraints. Numerical thresholds, format validity, and fixed-pattern detection all work reliably. The exception — negation patterns — can be handled by routing them to the per-requirement LLM. Caveat: "wide" applies to numerical/format constraints; for functional/semantic requirements, real-agent-authored evidence is far harsher — C1 collapses under agent vocabulary drift.

Fourth, the negation blind spot in regex evaluation is the same problem as the DPI blind spot, one level down. A regex that matches "write-invalidation" in "not write-invalidation" is making the same error as an LLM that reads "all tests pass" and misses that the wrong test suite was run. Both are pattern-matchers that can't distinguish "mentioned" from "satisfied."

6. Summary

Experiment Question Answer
Phase 1 (12 scenarios) Text channel vs filesystem channel Complementary blind spots; combined = 88.9% detection / 91.7% overall
Phase 2 (7 scenarios) Free-text vs contract regex vs per-req LLM Per-req = 100% detection; contract regex = 85.7% at zero cost
Combined (19 scenarios) What catches the surfaced-deviation gap? Per-requirement LLM (C2), when the deviation appears in evidence text; a non-surfaced deviation (genuine DPI bound) is uncloseable from any text channel

The architectural conclusion: replace the single free-text LLM evaluation (old L2) with a three-stage pipeline — evidence gate (file system) → contract regex (text patterns) → per-requirement LLM (semantic checks). Each stage catches what the previous one misses. The combination narrows the gap on every scenario we constructed — every named evasion becomes a deterministic catch — but it does not close it. Two residues remain. (1) Unenumerated evasions in word-space: a fresh synonym or reframed justification clears the regex layers until you name it — the ratchet turns, the gap doesn't vanish. (2) The genuine DPI bound: a deviation the producer never surfaces in any text channel is invisible to every text-reading mechanism, regex or LLM. That floor lives in argument-space — exercising the code path and observing the side effect on the referent the claim names — which is outside this pipeline and outside any text channel.

  • Phase 2: contract-comparison-test.py — 7 scenarios, 3 mechanisms
  • skillgate source: npm and GitHub (v0.5.0, the version described; now at 0.6.x)

Decompose "done" into individual requirements and check each one separately. 3.1 Design 7 scenarios, each gated by a 5-requirement contract — five share a rate-limiting middleware contract, the other two reuse the Phase 1 CI-pipeline baselines: REQ-1: IP-level rate limiting → evidence: test-output.txt REQ-2: User-level rate limiting → evidence: test-output.txt REQ-3: Write-invalidation on write → evidence: diff-review.md (review text) REQ-4: Coverage ≥ 85% → evidence: coverage-summary.txt REQ-5: Lint 0 errors → evidence: lint-report.txt Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Three evaluators: C0 (free-text LLM): Same as Phase 1 Channel A — LLM reads everything and judges holistically. C1 (contract regex): For each requirement, read the evidence file and regex match a pattern. No model. Zero cost. C2 (per-requirement LLM): For each requirement, ask the LLM: "Does this evidence prove requirement N?" Then check whether ALL pass. Cost: ~1s per requirement instead of ~1s for one holistic call. 3.2 Results Metric C0 (free-text) C1 (contract regex) C2 (per-req LLM) Overall accuracy 42.9% 85.7% 85.7% Detection rate 20.0% 80.0% 100% False acceptance 4 1 0 False rejection 0 0 1 Per-item accuracy — 88.6% 82.9% The numbers tell a clear story. C0 (free-text LLM) collapses on the hardest set. 4 of 5 non-compliant scenarios were missed. The LLM read the agent's output, saw "tests pass, lint clean, coverage 92%," and declared it done — even when the core requirement (write-invalidation) was missing. Same mechanism as Phase 1's SC10: the LLM is doing an impression judgment, not a line-by-line audit. C1 (contract regex) is surprisingly effective for a zero-cost solution. 85.7% overall, 80% detection. The one failure is instructive: SC10a (the write-invalidation gap again). The diff-review.md says "keys expire via TTL, not write-invalidation" — and the regex write.?invalidat matched the word "write-invalidation" in the negation. C1 has a "negation blind spot": it matches the mention of a requirement, not its satisfaction. But C1 is excellent on numerical and format constraints: Pattern type Reliability Example Numerical comparison ✅ `(8[5-9]\ Fixed-format text ✅ {% raw %}0\s+errors for lint Functional keywords ⚠️ Naming-sensitive (purgeCacheOnWrite vs write-invalidation) Negated mentions ❌ "not write-invalidation" matches write.?invalidat C2 (per-requirement LLM) achieves 100% detection rate — the only mechanism in either experiment to catch every non-compliant scenario. It works because forcing the LLM to judge one requirement at a time prevents the "everything looks fine" gestalt from overriding the missing-item signal. On SC10a (the semantic gap), the per-requirement LLM correctly rejected REQ-3 — it noted the evidence explicitly describes TTL expiration instead of write-invalidation, so the requirement isn't satisfied. The same LLM in C0 mode on the same scenario judged the work done: tests pass, lint clean, coverage 92% — all requirements met. The difference isn't model capability. It's the same model, same temperature, different framing. The holistic frame asks "is this good?" The per-item frame asks "is this specific thing proven?" C2's one false rejection (SC10c — which was genuinely compliant) was on REQ-3: the per-req LLM rejected write-invalidation because the diff-review.md "only mentions it, doesn't prove it with code." This is arguably correct behavior — a review file shouldn't be sufficient evidence for code-level requirements. The false rejection exposed a contract design issue, not an evaluator issue. 3.3 Contract regex failure pattern The C1 negation blind spot deserves deeper analysis because it mirrors the Data Processing Inequality at the regex level: Input Regex Match? Correct? "Keys expire via TTL, not write-invalidation" write.?invalidat YES ❌ False pass "Coverage: 72.3%" `(8[5-9]\ 90+)\%` NO "Implemented purgeCacheOnWrite" purge.*write YES ✅ Correct pass The numerical constraint (85%+) is immune to the negation problem because a number below threshold is factually wrong regardless of context. The keyword constraint (write.?invalidat) is vulnerable because the regex can't tell the difference between "I implemented X" and "I didn't implement X." A regex constraint can be strengthened with negative lookahead — (?!not.*)write.?invalidat — but this quickly becomes fragile and regex-specific. The practical fix is to route semantic requirements (where negation matters) to C2 (per-req LLM) and reserve C1 for numerical and format constraints. This makes C1 a ratchet on named evasions, not a closure. Every pattern you write is one lie permanently caught — but each unenumerated semantic dimension (a fresh synonym, a reframed justification like "the cache converges via eventual-consistency guarantees without explicit invalidation") is an isomorphic gap C1 cannot see, because it lives in word-space and you didn't name those words. C2 widens the ratchet: it reads the same text the producer wrote, so it catches any deviation that surfaces in the evidence. But C2 shares the text channel — a deviation the producer never puts into any evidence file is invisible to C2 as well. 4. Synthesis: The Evidence Gate Pipeline Putting Phase 1 and Phase 2 together produces a three-layer post-L1 pipeline that replaces the single L2 free-text LLM from Part 6: output file │ L0 → L0e → L1 │ pass ┌─────────▼──────────┐ │ Evidence Gate │ file exists + non-empty │ (deterministic) │ ~0ms └─────────┬──────────┘ │ pass ┌─────────▼──────────┐ │ C1 Contract Regex │ per-requirement regex │ (deterministic) │ best for: numerical, format └─────────┬──────────┘ │ │ UNCLEAR ALL PASS │ │ ┌────▼───┐ │ │ C2 Per- │ │ │ Req LLM │ │ │ ~1s/REQ │ │ └────┬───┘ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ │ │ L3 ◄─────┘ │ (shared)│ └─────────┘ Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 4.1 When to use each path No contract defined (no evidence_gates config): Traditional L0 → L0e → L1 → L2 (free-text LLM) → L3 Same as Part 6 architecture. Works when there's no predefined set of verifiable requirements. Contract defined (with evidence_gates): L0 → L0e → L1 → Evidence Gate → C1 → (C2 if needed) → L3 C1 handles numerical and format constraints deterministically (zero cost) C2 handles semantic constraints per-requirement (higher cost, but higher detection rate) The contract defines requirements with a type field: "regex" for C1, "llm" for C2 The combined channel performance: Mechanism Detection rate Cost per scenario C0 free-text LLM (old L2) 20% ~1s Evidence Gate (Phase 1 Channel B) 66.7% ~0ms C1 contract regex 80.0% ~0ms C2 per-req LLM 100% ~1s × N_req Combined A+B (Phase 1, any reject) 88.9% ~1s Rates are per-mechanism on each experiment's own scenario set — Phase 1 (12 scenarios) for Evidence Gate and A+B, Phase 2 (7 scenarios) for C0/C1/C2 — not a single cumulative run. 4.2 The remaining gap One scenario is the hardest across both experiments: SC10/SC10a, the semantic compliance gap — structurally complete output, correct evidence files, all tests pass, adequate coverage, coherent self-review, but the output doesn't satisfy the actual requirement. In Phase 1 it evaded both channels (A and B both passed SC10). In Phase 2, C2 caught SC10a — because the deviation surfaced in the review text ("keys expire via TTL, not write-invalidation"). C2 reads the same text channel the producer wrote, so a deviation the producer put into words is detectable. The case no text-channel mechanism can catch — the genuine DPI bound — is the opposite: a deviation the producer never surfaces in any evidence file. If the agent omits write-invalidation entirely and never mentions TTL, the missing requirement leaves no trace in any text the evaluator can read. Regex can't match what isn't there; an LLM reading the evidence can't notice an absence it has no signal for. This is the theoretically provable blind spot the Data Processing Inequality names: the evaluator's information is a subset of the producer's output, and an absence the producer never writes down is absent from that subset too. The fixes are all outside the evaluation channel — and they're the prescription René named in the original comment, which the experiments backfill: Human review on material calls — a person reads the requirement vs the implementation A hard step budget — the agent runs out of steps before it can simulate compliance Deterministic checks on what is actually binary — skillgate's VPS pre-receive hook cannot be fooled by plausible output Skillgate implements the third. The first two are a human reviewer and the orchestrator's step limit. 4.3 Implementation The pipeline described here has been integrated into forge-verify's content-verify.mjs as an optional evidence gate mode. Configured via .forge/content-verify.json: { "task": "Implement rate limiting middleware", "files": ["src/rate-limit.ts"], "evidence_gates": { "evidence_dir": ".skillgate/evidence", "requirements": [ { "id": "REQ-1", "desc": "IP level rate limiting", "evidence_file": "test-output.txt", "pattern": "(?i)(RateLimiter.*IP|isRateLimited.*IP)", "type": "regex" }, { "id": "REQ-2", "desc": "Write-invalidation on cache writes", "evidence_file": "diff-review.md", "type": "llm" }, { "id": "REQ-3", "desc": "Coverage >= 85%", "evidence_file": "coverage-summary.txt", "pattern": "(8[5-9]|90+)%", "type": "regex" } ] } } Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode When evidence_gates is configured, the pipeline runs the evidence gate → C1 (regex requirements) → C2 (LLM requirements) → L3 path. When absent, it falls back to the traditional L0 → L2 → L3 path. Backward compatible — existing configurations don't need changes. 5. What the Two Experiments Established First, the channel you evaluate through determines what you can detect. An LLM reading text catches content-level failures that a filesystem check cannot — fabricated evidence, stale dates, implausible narratives. A filesystem check catches mechanical gaps cheaply and deterministically, and in this run the LLM caught those too — redundant coverage, not complementarity. The divergence is narrow but real: filesystem accepts fabricated and stale evidence at face value, while the LLM accepted the agent's "no test needed" rationalization. Neither channel alone is sufficient, and the shared blind spot is provably uncloseable from either channel alone. Second, per-requirement evaluation outperforms holistic evaluation by a wide margin. The same LLM, same temperature, same evidence — but asking "does this evidence prove requirement N?" instead of "is the work done?" raised detection rate from 20% to 100%. The frame matters more than the model. Third, contract regex is a practical zero-cost filter for a surprisingly wide set of constraints. Numerical thresholds, format validity, and fixed-pattern detection all work reliably. The exception — negation patterns — can be handled by routing them to the per-requirement LLM. Caveat: "wide" applies to numerical/format constraints; for functional/semantic requirements, real-agent-authored evidence is far harsher — C1 collapses under agent vocabulary drift. Fourth, the negation blind spot in regex evaluation is the same problem as the DPI blind spot, one level down. A regex that matches "write-invalidation" in "not write-invalidation" is making the same error as an LLM that reads "all tests pass" and misses that the wrong test suite was run. Both are pattern-matchers that can't distinguish "mentioned" from "satisfied." 6. Summary Experiment Question Answer Phase 1 (12 scenarios) Text channel vs filesystem channel Complementary blind spots; combined = 88.9% detection / 91.7% overall Phase 2 (7 scenarios) Free-text vs contract regex vs per-req LLM Per-req = 100% detection; contract regex = 85.7% at zero cost Combined (19 scenarios) What catches the surfaced-deviation gap? Per-requirement LLM (C2), when the deviation appears in evidence text; a non-surfaced deviation (genuine DPI bound) is uncloseable from any text channel The architectural conclusion: replace the single free-text LLM evaluation (old L2) with a three-stage pipeline — evidence gate (file system) → contract regex (text patterns) → per-requirement LLM (semantic checks). Each stage catches what the previous one misses. The combination narrows the gap on every scenario we constructed — every named evasion becomes a deterministic catch — but it does not close it. Two residues remain. (1) Unenumerated evasions in word-space: a fresh synonym or reframed justification clears the regex layers until you name it — the ratchet turns, the gap doesn't vanish. (2) The genuine DPI bound: a deviation the producer never surfaces in any text channel is invisible to every text-reading mechanism, regex or LLM. That floor lives in argument-space — exercising the code path and observing the side effect on the referent the claim names — which is outside this pipeline and outside any text channel. sentences.zh: 本文比较了验证层的两种相互竞争的设计——一种通过 LLM 读取文本，一种通过确定性检查读取文件系统——并展示了为什么两者都不能单独工作，以及为什么组合方法会缩小差距而不缩小差距：每个命名的逃避都成为确定性的捕获，而未列举的其余部分则保持不明确，并路由给人类，而不是默默地通过。

blocks.html_en: First, the channel you evaluate through determines what you can detect. An LLM reading text catches content-level failures that a filesystem check cannot — fabricated evidence, stale dates, implausible narratives. A filesystem check catches mechanical gaps cheaply and deterministically, and in this run the LLM caught those too — redundant coverage, not complementarity. The divergence is narrow but real: filesystem accepts fabricated and stale evidence at face value, while the LLM accepted the agent's "no test needed" rationalization. Neither channel alone is sufficient, and the shared blind spot is provably uncloseable from either channel alone.

content_html_zh:
渠道差距：为什么你的法学硕士法官是一只眼睛瞎了

主体决定论错觉（第 8 部分）

第 6 部分以根据社区矫正构建的功能性分层管道结束。 然后，第 7 部分修复了升级触发器：仅分歧将人类引导至安全模糊集，并自动传递自信错误集。 L0/L1 确定性过滤，L2 处理语义残差，L3 检测分歧——加上用于一致遗漏的类绊线。 这比之前的情况要好。 但它仍然存在一个基本的设计缺陷，我只是在阅读了实现相反设计选择的工具后才意识到这一缺陷。

本文比较了验证层的两种相互竞争的设计——一种通过 LLM 读取文本，一种通过确定性检查读取文件系统——并展示了为什么两者都不能单独工作，以及为什么组合方法会缩小差距而不缩小差距：每个命名的逃避都成为确定性的捕获，而未列举的其余部分则保持不明确，并路由给人类，而不是默默地通过。

1. 改变框架的评论

该系列上线后，René Zander（@reneza on dev.to）留下了以下内容：

“词汇重叠、温度 0 判断和阶段门都试图进行概率判断调用（‘这是完成了吗’，‘这是一个新任务’）返回一个二进制事实，并且将其装在代码中并不会改变它的本质。”

他们说该系列中的每个“确定性修复”都是语义决策的确定性包装。 词汇重叠阈值、温度 0 评估、相位门形式主义——所有这些都将概率判断放入看起来确定性的代码结构中，但潜在的决策仍然是模型输出。 代码并没有让判断更加可靠；这使得不可靠性更难被发现。

评论者没有说出它的名字，但他们描述的是数据处理不平等：当评估者与生产者共享相同的通信通道（读/写文本）时，评估者可用的信息是生产者输出的子集。 如果文本中没有出现偏差，评估者（人类或法学硕士）就无法检测到它。

他们创建了一个工具来实现替代方案：skillgate。

1.1 替代方案：技能门

Skillgate（npm 上的@reneza/skillgate）是一个确定性的、独立于模型的门，它检查文件系统而不是读取模型的输出。 它的论点是：不要问任务是否完成，而要问证据是否存在。

实现是最小的——一个紧凑的 TypeScript 包，具有​​两个外部依赖项（一个 YAML 解析器和一个 glob 匹配器）。 其闸门类型：

  • 文件存在 — 路径存在
  • 证据 — 文件存在且非空
  • 非空 — 路径中的目录至少包含 min 条目
  • 不存在 - 正则表达式模式不会出现在匹配的文件中
  • file-contains — 文件与正则表达式匹配
  • 命令 — shell 命令退出 0
  • 指令同步 — 指令文件没有漂移（LCS 相似度 ≥ 0.95）

请注意缺少什么：没有法学硕士法官。 每个门都是文件系统上的纯函数。 相同的磁盘状态，相同的判决。 总是。

执行机制是 Claude Code 中的 PreToolUse 钩子，它拦截 git commit、git push、npmpublish、运行门，并在任何门失败时以代码 2 退出（阻止工具调用）。 代理看到失败消息并可以尝试修复，但它不能覆盖门 - 门位于模型的控制流之外。

三个部署层，每个层都强制执行相同的 .skillgate/done.yaml：

Layer Where 谁控制它 可绕过吗？
Soft 克劳德代码 PreToolUse 挂钩 项目配置 模型可修改挂钩
Soft 预提交 git hook 本地仓库 git commit --无验证
Hard 自托管 VPS 上的预接收挂钩 服务器管理员 代理无法登录盒子

硬层是架构创新：预接收钩子具体化推送的树，针对权威的 .skillgate/done.yaml（位于服务器上，而不是存储库中）运行技能门检查，并在任何门失败时拒绝推送。 代理无法通过 git-push 方式通过门，因为门在服务器上完成 git Push 后运行。

这不是一个理论设计。 它作为 v0.5.0 发布，源代码可以在 GitHub 上读取。

1.2 Skillgate 的不同之处

ReqForge 的 forge-verify 和 Skillgate 解决了同样的问题——“工作真的完成了吗？” ——通过完全不同的渠道：

方面 伪造验证（L0-L3） 技能门
渠道 Text — 读取模型输出 文件系统——检查工件
评估员 代码+法学硕士 仅代码
DPI 限制 是 - 通过文本评估文本 否 - 通过工件评估操作
判断方差 LLM温度、型号版本、提示 零——纯函数
Scope 生产了什么 它被生产出来了
执行 停时钩（软） 预收钩（硬）

这个对比暴露了我应该在第 6 部分中提出但没有提出的问题：

如果我们有两个完全不同的渠道来评估合规性，那么每个渠道都发现了另一个渠道错过的东西，而两者加起来仍然错过了什么？

这个问题推动了两轮实验。

2. 第一阶段：渠道比较

2.1 设计

代理声称已完成任务的 12 种场景。 每个场景都有：

  1. 代理输出文本 - 代理所说的内容
  2. 证据文件——哪些工件文件存在（或不存在）
  3. 事实真相——代理人是否真的遵守了规定

两个评估者，每个评估者仅限于自己的渠道：

  • 通道 A（通道内）：LLM（deepseek-v4-flash，温度 0）读取代理的输出文本 + 任何证据文件内容。 决定：“工作完成了吗？” 每个场景 N=3 票，多数决定。
  • 通道B（带外）：文件系统检查——对于每个所需的证据文件，它是否存在并且是否非空？ 不涉及法学硕士。 纯函数。

这 12 种场景涵盖：完全合规、证据缺失、空证据、捏造证据、部分证据、陈旧证据、语义合规差距和代理合理化。

2.2 结果

公制 通道A（法学硕士文本） 通道 B（文件系统）
整体准确度 83.3% 75.0%
检出率 77.8% 66.7%
错误接受 (FA) 2 3
错误拒绝（FR） 0 0

每个渠道都有零错误拒绝——当他们标记某件事时，它是真实的。 区别在于他们错过了什么。

频道 A 发现了频道 B 错过的信息：

  • 捏造的证据 (SC04)：证据文件的内容类似于“所有测试都通过了！” 但没有真正的测试输出。 频道 A 阅读了内容，但因内容过于模糊而拒绝了。 通道 B 表示“文件存在且非空 → PASS”。
  • 陈旧证据 (SC07)：昨天的证据文件声称“已清除 3 个文件”，而特工日志声称“今天已清除 5 个文件”。 频道 A 注意到日期不匹配。 通道 B 说“文件存在→通过”。

频道 B 发现了频道 A 错过的信息：

  • 仅审阅 (SC11)：代理编写了代码审阅但未运行测试。 它的自我审查是合理的：“不需要测试运行——改变很小。” 频道 A 认为这个推理很有说服力（2/3 票通过）。 通道 B 检查：test-output.txt 不存在 → 拒绝。

最有启发性的场景——语义差距（SC10）：

  • 代理的任务：“实施具有关键写入无效功能的速率限制中间件。”
  • 代理制作：具有 IP/用户级别限制的 RateLimiter 类，Redis 存储，24 次通过测试，92% 覆盖率。 一切看起来都很完整。
  • 不存在：写入无效——代理的自我审查从未提及它。 审查看起来像是一次干净的交接：实现了类，添加了存储后端，测试通过，lint 干净。
  • 通道 A：3/3 通过 — 确信工作已完成。
  • 通道 B：通过 — 所有证据文件均存在且非空。

两个通道都错过了同一个：结构完美但不符合要求的输出。

2.3 盲点图

失效模式 频道A（文字） 通道 B（文件系统）
证据缺失 ✅ ✅
空证据 ✅ ✅
捏造内容 ✅ ❌
陈旧的内容 ✅ ❌
部分证据 ✅ ✅
代理合理化（“无需测试”） ❌ ✅
语义差距（DPI 限制） ❌ ❌

组合（A 或 B 拒绝）捕获 9 个不合规场景中的 8 个（检测率为 88.9%），并正确通过所有 3 个合规场景 — 总体正确判定为 11/12（91.7%）。 唯一的共同盲点是语义差距——事实证明，仅通过文本或文件系统证据是无法检测到这一点的。

3. 第二阶段：合同验证

第一阶段的盲点地图表明：为了缩小剩余的差距，我们需要检查证据的内容，而不仅仅是证据的存在。 但如何呢？ 通道 A（法学硕士阅读文本）在这种情况下已经失败了。

答案是：不要要求法学硕士来评判整体情况。 将“完成”分解为单独的需求并单独检查每一项。

3.1 设计

7 个场景，每个场景都由 5 个需求合约控制——五个共享一个速率限制中间件合约，另外两个重用第一阶段 CI 管道基线：

REQ-1: IP-level rate limiting       → evidence: test-output.txt
REQ-2: User-level rate limiting     → evidence: test-output.txt  
REQ-3: Write-invalidation on write  → evidence: diff-review.md (review text)
REQ-4: Coverage ≥ 85%               → evidence: coverage-summary.txt
REQ-5: Lint 0 errors                → evidence: lint-report.txt

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

三位评审员：

  • C0（自由文本法学硕士）：与第一阶段通道 A 相同 - 法学硕士阅读所有内容并进行整体判断。
  • C1（合同正则表达式）：对于每个需求，阅读证据文件并使用正则表达式匹配模式。 没有型号。 零成本。
  • C2（按要求的法学硕士）：对于每项要求，询问法学硕士：“此证据是否证明要求 N？” 然后检查是否全部通过。 成本：每个需求约 1 秒，而不是一次整体调用约 1 秒。

3.2 结果

公制 C0（自由文本） C1（合同正则表达式） C2（按要求法学硕士）
整体准确度 42.9% 85.7% 85.7%
检出率 20.0% 80.0% 100%
错误接受 4 1 0
错误拒绝 0 0 1
每件商品的准确度 — 88.6% 82.9%

数字说明了一个清晰的故事。

C0（自由文本法学硕士）在最难的设置上崩溃了。 5 个不合规场景中有 4 个被遗漏。 LLM 读取了代理的输出，看到“测试通过，lint 干净，覆盖率 92%”，并宣布它已完成 - 即使核心要求（写入无效）缺失。 与第一阶段 SC10 的机制相同：LLM 正在进行印象判断，而不是逐行审核。

C1（契约正则表达式）对于零成本解决方案非常有效。 总体为 85.7%，检测率为 80%。 一个失败具有启发性：SC10a（再次出现写入无效间隙）。 diff-review.md 说“密钥通过 TTL 过期，而不是 write-invalidation”——并且正则表达式 write.?invalidat 与否定中的单词“write-invalidation”匹配。 C1 有一个“否定盲点”：它匹配某个需求的提及，而不是它的满足。

但 C1 在数字和格式限制方面表现出色：

图案类型 可靠性 例子
数值比较 ✅ `(8[5-9]\
固定格式文本 ✅ {% raw %}0\s+ lint 错误
功能性关键词 ⚠️ 命名敏感（purgeCacheOnWrite 与 write-invalidation）
否定提及 ❌ “not write-invalidation” 匹配 write.?invalidat

C2（按要求的法学硕士）实现了 100% 的检测率——这是这两个实验中捕获所有不合规场景的唯一机制。 它之所以有效，是因为强制法学硕士一次判断一项要求可以防止“一切看起来都很好”的格式塔覆盖缺失项目的信号。

在 SC10a（语义差距）上，按要求的 LLM 正确拒绝了 REQ-3 — 它指出证据明确描述了 TTL 过期而不是写入无效，因此不满足要求。

在同一场景中，C0 模式下的同一法学硕士对完成的工作进行了判断：测试通过、lint 干净、覆盖率 92% — 满足所有要求。

区别不在于模型能力。 相同的模型，相同的温度，不同的框架。 整体框架问“这好吗？” 每个项目的框架询问“这个特定的事情是否被证明？”

C2 的一个错误拒绝（SC10c — 真正符合要求）是在 REQ-3 上：per-req LLM 拒绝了写入无效，因为 diff-review.md“只提到了它，没有用代码证明它。” 这可以说是正确的行为——审查文件不应该成为代码级要求的充分证据。 虚假拒绝暴露了合同设计问题，而不是评估者问题。

3.3 合约正则表达式失败模式

C1 否定盲点值得更深入的分析，因为它反映了正则表达式级别的数据处理不平等：

Input Regex Match? 正确的？
“密钥通过 TTL 过期，而不是写入失效” 写.?无效 YES ❌ 误传
“覆盖率：72.3%” `(8[5-9]\ 90+)\%` NO
“已实现 purgeCacheOnWrite” 清除。*写入 YES ✅ 正确通过

数值约束 (85%+) 不受否定问题的影响，因为无论上下文如何，低于阈值的数字实际上都是错误的。 关键字约束 (write.?invalidat) 很容易受到攻击，因为正则表达式无法区分“我实现了 X”和“我没有实现 X”。

正则表达式约束可以通过负向前瞻（(?!not.*)write.?invalidat）来加强，但这很快就会变得脆弱且特定于正则表达式。 实际的解决方法是将语义需求（否定很重要）路由到 C2（每个需求的 LLM）并保留 C1 来满足数字和格式约束。

这使得 C1 成为命名逃避的棘轮，而不是关闭。 你写的每一个模式都是一个永远被抓住的谎言——但每一个未列举的语义维度（一个新的同义词，一个重新构建的理由，比如“缓存通过最终一致性保证收敛，没有显式失效”）是一个 C1 无法看到的同构间隙，因为它存在于单词空间中，而你没有命名这些单词。 C2 扩大了棘轮：它读取制作人编写的相同文本，因此它可以捕获证据中出现的任何偏差。 但 C2 共享文本通道——制作人从未将其放入任何证据文件中的偏差对 C2 来说也是不可见的。

4. 综合：证据门管道

将第 1 阶段和第 2 阶段放在一起生成一个三层后 L1 管道，取代第 6 部分中的单个 L2 自由文本 LLM：

                   output file
                        │

4.1 何时使用每条路径

没有定义合约（没有evidence_gates配置）：

  • 传统 L0 → L0e → L1 → L2（自由文本 LLM）→ L3
  • 与第 6 部分架构相同。 在没有预定义的可验证需求集时有效。

合约定义（使用evidence_gates）：

  • L0→L0e→L1→证据门→C1→（C2，如果需要）→L3
  • C1 确定性地处理数字和格式约束（零成本）
  • C2 根据需求处理语义约束（成本较高，但检测率较高）
  • 合同使用类型字段定义需求：“regex”代表 C1，“llm”代表 C2

组合通道性能：

4.2 剩余间隙

两个实验中最难的一个场景是：SC10/SC10a，语义合规性差距——结构完整的输出、正确的证据文件、所有测试通过、足够的覆盖范围、连贯的自我审查，但输出不满足实际要求。 在第一阶段，它避开了两个通道（A 和 B 都通过了 SC10）。 在第 2 阶段，C2 捕获了 SC10a——因为评论文本中出现了偏差（“密钥通过 TTL 过期，而不是写入失效”）。 C2 读取制作者编写的相同文本通道，因此制作者输入的文字的偏差是可以检测到的。

任何文本通道机制都无法捕获的情况（真正的 DPI 限制）则相反：生产者从未在任何证据文件中显示出偏差。 如果代理完全忽略写入无效并且从不提及 TTL，则缺失的要求不会在评估者可以读取的任何文本中留下任何痕迹。 正则表达式无法匹配不存在的内容；阅读证据的法学硕士无法注意到没有信号的缺席。 这就是理论上可证明的数据处理不等式所称的盲点：评估者的信息是生产者输出的子集，而生产者从未记录下来的缺失也不在该子集中。

这些修复都在评估渠道之外——它们是 René 在原始评论中指定的处方，实验对此进行了回补：

  • 对材料调用进行人工审查——一个人阅读需求与实施
  • 困难的步骤预算——代理在模拟合规性之前就用完了步骤
  • 对实际二进制内容进行确定性检查——skillgate 的 VPS 预接收挂钩不会被看似合理的输出所欺骗

Skillgate 实现了第三个。 前两个是人工审核员和协调器的步数限制。

5. 两个实验证实了什么

首先，您评估的渠道决定了您可以检测到的内容。 法学硕士阅读文本可以捕获文件系统检查无法捕获的内容级故障——捏造的证据、陈旧的日期、难以置信的叙述。 文件系统检查可以廉价且确定性地捕获机械间隙，在本次运行中，法学硕士也捕获了这些间隙——冗余覆盖，而不是互补性。 分歧虽小但真实：文件系统从表面上接受捏造的陈旧证据，而法学硕士则接受代理人“无需测试”的合理化。 单独使用任何一个通道都是不够的，并且事实证明，仅使用任一通道都无法关闭共享盲点。

其次，按需求评估大大优于整体评估。 相同的法学硕士、相同的温度、相同的证据——但要问“这个证据是否证明了要求 N？” 而不是“工作完成了吗？” 检出率从20%提高到100%。 框架比模型更重要。

第三，合约正则表达式是一种实用的零成本过滤器，适用于范围广泛的约束。 数值阈值、格式有效性和固定模式检测都可靠地工作。 例外情况——否定模式——可以通过将它们路由到按要求的 LLM 来处理。 警告：“宽”适用于数字/格式限制；对于功能/语义要求，真实代理编写的证据要严格得多——C1 在代理词汇漂移的情况下崩溃。

第四，正则表达式求值中的否定盲点与DPI盲点是同一个问题，只是低一级。 与“不写无效”中的“写无效”匹配的正则表达式与读取“所有测试通过”的 LLM 会犯相同的错误，并且会错过运行了错误的测试套件。 两者都是模式匹配器，无法区分“提及”和“满意”。

架构结论：用三阶段管道取代单一自由文本 LLM 评估（旧的 L2）——证据门（文件系统）→ 合约正则表达式（文本模式）→ 按需求 LLM（语义检查）。 每个阶段都会抓住前一个阶段错过的东西。 这种组合缩小了我们构建的每个场景的差距——每个命名的逃避都成为一个确定性的捕获——但它并没有缩小差距。 剩下两个残留物。 (1) 单词空间中未列举的回避：一个新的同义词或重新构建的理由会清除正则表达式层，直到你说出它的名字 - 棘轮转动，间隙不会消失。 (2) 真正的 DPI 界限：生产者从未在任何文本通道中出现的偏差对于每个文本阅读机制、正则表达式或 LLM 都是不可见的。 该楼层位于参数空间中 - 执行代码路径并观察声明名称所指对象的副作用 - 位于该管道之外和任何文本通道之外。
